Take the bottom-left grid point as \((0,0)\), with \(x\) increasing rightward and \(y\) upward. Let the endpoints of the vertical black segment be
\[
A=(1,4),\qquad B=(1,2),
\]
and those of the horizontal black segment be
\[
C=(3,2),\qquad D=(5,2).
\]

The candidate points are
\[
X=(3,4),\quad Y=(2,3),\quad Z=(1,1),\quad T=(2,1).
\]

### Check \(X\)
Relative to \(X\),
\[
A-X=(-2,0),\qquad B-X=(-2,-2).
\]
A \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation sends these to
\[
(0,-2)=C-X,\qquad (2,-2)=D-X.
\]
Thus \(X\) maps the vertical segment onto the horizontal segment.

### Check \(T\)
Relative to \(T\),
\[
B-T=(-1,1),\qquad A-T=(-1,3).
\]
A \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation sends these to
\[
(1,1)=C-T,\qquad (3,1)=D-T.
\]
Thus \(T\) also works.

### Eliminate \(Y\) and \(Z\)
A rotation preserves the distances from its center to corresponding endpoints:

- From \(Y\), the distances to the vertical endpoints are \(\{\sqrt2,\sqrt2\}\), while those to the horizontal endpoints are \(\{\sqrt2,\sqrt{10}\}\).
- From \(Z\), the distances are \(\{3,1\}\) and \(\{\sqrt5,\sqrt{17}\}\), respectively.

Neither distance set matches, so neither \(Y\) nor \(Z\) can be the center.

\[
\boxed{\text{C: }X\text{ and }T}
\]
